docs.title: VAE
docs.text:
A VAE pays for two things at once: reconstructing its input, and keeping its latent codes close to a prior one can sample from. This report follows that tug of war. Exercise 1 trains a real VAE on MNIST (latent dimension \(d = 16\)) and logs the two terms of the loss separately; Exercise 2 repeats the experiment with \(d = 2\), a latent space that can be drawn, to see what the prior buys and what it costs.

Everything VAE-specific is written by hand in code/vae.py: the reparameterisation, both terms of the loss and the sampling. PyTorch supplies autograd, nn.Linear and Adam; torchvision only loads MNIST; scikit-learn appears for a 15-nearest-neighbour probe and a confusion matrix, scipy for norm.ppf. Every loss value is in nats per image (summed over the 784 pixels or over the latent dimensions, averaged over the images). Seeds: torch.manual_seed(42) right before each model is built, the split generator seeded with 42, and torch.manual_seed(0) right before the prior samples of Figure 3. The test set is used only for the final numbers of each model, for the figures the statement defines on test images, and for the post-hoc analysis numbers of 2E (per-digit reconstruction, the 15-nearest-neighbour probe, the digit centroids, the random-pair distances), none of which feeds back into training or model choice.

python docs/exercises/vae/code/vae.py                 # self-check of the hand-written loss terms
python docs/exercises/vae/code/ex1_vae_mnist.py       # Exercise 1: Figures 1-3, results_ex1.json (about 1 minute on a CPU)
python docs/exercises/vae/code/ex2_latent_plane.py    # Exercise 2: Figures 4-6, results_ex2.json (about 1 minute)

MNIST is downloaded to code/data/ on the first run (not committed). Exercise 2 reads the \(d = 16\) checkpoint that Exercise 1 saves there, and runs Exercise 1 first if it is missing. Every number below is copied from code/results_ex1.json or code/results_ex2.json, which the two scripts write. Run on a clean copy of the code/ folder (no data/, no results), ex2_latent_plane.py alone reproduced both JSON files and all six figures byte for byte (same machine, 4 CPU threads; another CPU or thread count can move the last digits).

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text: A VAE on MNIST.

docs.title: A — Load and split the data
docs.text:
MNIST from torchvision with transforms.ToTensor() (pixels in \([0, 1]\)), each image flattened into a 784-vector. The 60 000 training images are split with the statement's call, unchanged except that the download folder "data" is str(DATA_DIR):

train_full = datasets.MNIST(str(DATA_DIR), train=True, download=True, transform=transforms.ToTensor())
test = datasets.MNIST(str(DATA_DIR), train=False, download=True, transform=transforms.ToTensor())
train, val = random_split(train_full, [50_000, 10_000],
                          generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(42))

That gives 50 000 training images and 10 000 validation images; the 10 000 official test images are the test set. The MNIST folder is code/data/, resolved from __file__ so the scripts run from any directory. ToTensor() is just uint8 / 255, so load_data() reads the same numbers straight from the dataset tensors (it asserts equality with the transform's output on the first image) instead of decoding 70 000 PIL images one by one.

train_vae() receives only X_train and X_val. The test tensors are loaded with the rest but first used after training, for the final numbers and for the figures the statement defines on test images; no decision during training looks at them.

docs.title: B — Build the model
docs.text:
Part Layers Encoder \(784 \to 512 \to 256\), ReLU after each Heads two linear layers \(256 \to d\): one for \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\), one for \(\log \boldsymbol{\sigma}^2\) Decoder \(d \to 256 \to 512 \to 784\), ReLU after the hidden layers, sigmoid at the output

With \(d = 16\) the model has 1 079 600 parameters (asserted by selfcheck()). The loss per image, summed over pixels and over latent dimensions, with \(\beta = 1\), averaged over the images of the batch:

\[ L = \underbrace{-\sum_{j=1}^{784} \Big[x_j \log \hat{x}_j + (1 - x_j) \log (1 - \hat{x}_j)\Big]}_{\text{reconstruction (BCE)}} + \beta \cdot \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{d} \left(\mu_i^2 + \sigma_i^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_i^2\right)}_{\text{KL}} \]
  • The head outputs \(\log \sigma^2\), not \(\sigma\). A linear layer returns any real number; \(\sigma = \exp(\tfrac{1}{2}\log\sigma^2)\) is positive by construction, with no clamp or softplus, and \(\log\sigma^2\) is what the KL formula contains.
  • Reparameterisation. \(z = \mu + \sigma \odot \varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\), written as mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * torch.randn_like(mu). The noise is an input, not a function of the parameters, so autograd carries the gradient of the reconstruction through \(z\) into both heads.
  • KL in closed form. For \(q(z \mid x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \operatorname{diag}\sigma^2)\) against the prior \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\) the KL is the sum over the dimensions of \(\tfrac{1}{2}(\mu_i^2 + \sigma_i^2 - 1 - \log\sigma_i^2)\), written out in kl_term(). It is zero exactly when \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma = 1\).
  • BCE here, squared error in the lecture. Both are \(-\log p(x \mid z)\) under a pixel likelihood: a Gaussian gives the squared error, a Bernoulli gives the BCE. The sigmoid output is a probability per pixel and MNIST pixels are nearly 0 or 1, so the Bernoulli fits.
  • F.binary_cross_entropy(..., reduction="sum") divided by the batch size, never "mean". This is the form the statement prescribes for the reconstruction term. mean would also divide by the 784 pixels and shrink the reconstruction 784-fold against the KL: a silent \(\beta \approx 784\), which pushes \(q(z \mid x)\) onto the prior and collapses the code. The per-image sum also keeps the units (nats per image) the statement's reference values are in.
  • Checked, not assumed. python vae.py asserts that the KL is 0 at \(\mu = 0, \sigma = 1\), 0.5 at \(\mu = 1, \sigma = 1\) and equal to the closed-form value at \(\sigma = 2\); that recon_term equals the explicit \(-\sum_j [x_j \log p_j + (1 - x_j)\log(1 - p_j)] / B\); that gradients reach both heads through the reparameterisation; and the parameter count. No distribution objects and no library VAE class are used: both terms are plain tensor arithmetic.
"""Shared code for the VAE exercise: data, model, loss, training loop and evaluation.

Everything VAE-specific is written by hand in this file: the reparameterization trick, both terms
of the loss (Bernoulli/BCE reconstruction summed over the 784 pixels and the closed-form Gaussian KL
summed over the latent dimensions) and the sampling. PyTorch supplies only autograd, nn.Linear and
Adam; torchvision only downloads MNIST. No library VAE class and no distribution objects are used
(the statement forbids them).

Units: every loss value in this exercise is in nats per image (summed over pixels / latent
dimensions, averaged over the images).

Run `python vae.py` for a tiny self-check of the hand-written pieces.
"""
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.utils.data import random_split
from torchvision import datasets, transforms

# 4 threads keeps the CPU shareable, and it is the setting the report's numbers were produced with. Training is
# chaotic over the first epochs, so another thread count (or CPU) gives slightly different numbers (see the report).
torch.set_num_threads(4)

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
DATA_DIR = HERE / "data"          # MNIST download cache + d=16 checkpoint (gitignored)
FIG_DIR = HERE.parent / "figures"

SEED, EPOCHS, BATCH, LR, BETA = 42, 20, 128, 1e-3, 1.0


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 1A -- data
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
def load_data() -> dict:
    """MNIST as flat float32 tensors in [0, 1], split 50 000 / 10 000 / 10 000 (train / val / test)."""
    train_full = datasets.MNIST(str(DATA_DIR), train=True, download=True, transform=transforms.ToTensor())
    test = datasets.MNIST(str(DATA_DIR), train=False, download=True, transform=transforms.ToTensor())
    train, val = random_split(train_full, [50_000, 10_000],
                              generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(42))   # the statement's split

    # ToTensor() is just uint8 / 255; indexing the raw tensor gives the same numbers without
    # decoding 70 000 PIL images one by one.
    flat = lambda ds: ds.data.float().div(255).flatten(1)
    X, X_test = flat(train_full), flat(test)
    assert torch.equal(train_full[0][0].flatten(), X[0])          # identical to the ToTensor pipeline
    return dict(X_train=X[train.indices], y_train=train_full.targets[train.indices],
                X_val=X[val.indices], y_val=train_full.targets[val.indices],
                X_test=X_test, y_test=test.targets)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 1B -- model and loss
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
class VAE(nn.Module):
    """784 -> 512 -> 256 -> (mu, log sigma^2) in R^d  ->  256 -> 512 -> 784 (sigmoid)."""

    def __init__(self, d: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.enc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(512, 256), nn.ReLU())
        self.mu = nn.Linear(256, d)          # head 1: mean of q(z|x)
        # head 2: log sigma^2, not sigma. The layer output is any real number, and sigma = exp(logvar / 2)
        # is positive by construction (no clamp or softplus needed); log sigma^2 is also what the KL contains.
        self.logvar = nn.Linear(256, d)
        self.dec = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 512), nn.ReLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(512, 784), nn.Sigmoid())   # pixel probabilities in (0, 1)

    def encode(self, x):
        h = self.enc(x)
        return self.mu(h), self.logvar(h)

    def reparameterize(self, mu, logvar):
        """z = mu + sigma * eps, eps ~ N(0, I): the noise is an input, so gradients reach mu and logvar."""
        return mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * torch.randn_like(mu)

    def decode(self, z):
        return self.dec(z)

    def forward(self, x):
        mu, logvar = self.encode(x)
        z = self.reparameterize(mu, logvar)      # one sample per image
        return self.decode(z), mu, logvar


def recon_term(x_hat, x):
    """-log p(x|z) under a Bernoulli decoder: BCE summed over the 784 pixels, averaged over the batch."""
    # "sum" / batch, never "mean": mean would also divide by the 784 pixels, which shrinks this term
    # 784-fold against the KL, i.e. silently sets beta ~ 784 and pushes q(z|x) onto the prior (collapse).
    return F.binary_cross_entropy(x_hat, x, reduction="sum") / x.size(0)


def kl_term(mu, logvar):
    """KL( N(mu, sigma^2) || N(0, I) ) = 1/2 sum_i (mu_i^2 + sigma_i^2 - 1 - log sigma_i^2), batch average."""
    # Closed form for a diagonal Gaussian against the standard normal prior (no sampling, no library
    # helper). Summed over the d dimensions, averaged over the images: nats per image.
    return 0.5 * (mu.pow(2) + logvar.exp() - 1 - logvar).sum() / mu.size(0)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 1C -- evaluation and training
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
@torch.no_grad()
def evaluate(model, X):
    """(reconstruction, KL) in nats per image, one sampled z per image: a Monte-Carlo estimate of the ELBO."""
    model.eval()
    x_hat, mu, logvar = model(X)
    return recon_term(x_hat, X).item(), kl_term(mu, logvar).item()


@torch.no_grad()
def encode_all(model, X):
    """(mu, logvar) of every image; no sampling."""
    model.eval()
    mu, logvar = model.encode(X)
    return mu, logvar


def train_vae(d, X_train, X_val, epochs=EPOCHS, batch=BATCH, lr=LR, beta=BETA):
    """Adam, minibatches of 128. Returns the model and one dict per epoch with both loss terms,
    on the training set (average over the epoch) and on the validation set (end of the epoch).
    The test set never enters this function."""
    torch.manual_seed(SEED)                       # seed BEFORE building the model: it draws the init
    model = VAE(d)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    history = []
    for epoch in range(1, epochs + 1):
        model.train()
        order = torch.randperm(len(X_train))      # fresh shuffle every epoch (global RNG)
        s_rec = s_kl = 0.0
        for i in range(0, len(X_train), batch):
            x = X_train[order[i:i + batch]]
            x_hat, mu, logvar = model(x)
            rec, kl = recon_term(x_hat, x), kl_term(mu, logvar)
            opt.zero_grad()
            (rec + beta * kl).backward()          # L = reconstruction + beta * KL
            opt.step()
            s_rec += rec.item() * len(x)          # weight by batch size (the last batch has 80 images)
            s_kl += kl.item() * len(x)
        val_rec, val_kl = evaluate(model, X_val)
        history.append(dict(epoch=epoch, train_rec=s_rec / len(X_train), train_kl=s_kl / len(X_train),
                            val_rec=val_rec, val_kl=val_kl))
        print(f"d={d:<2d} epoch {epoch:2d}  train {history[-1]['train_rec']:7.2f} + {history[-1]['train_kl']:5.2f}"
              f"   val {val_rec:7.2f} + {val_kl:5.2f} = {val_rec + val_kl:7.2f}", flush=True)
    return model, history


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# small helpers
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
def tile(imgs, rows, cols):
    """(rows*cols, 784) -> one (rows*28, cols*28) picture, filled row by row."""
    return imgs.view(rows, cols, 28, 28).permute(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(rows * 28, cols * 28)


def selfcheck():
    z = torch.zeros(3, 4)
    assert kl_term(z, z).item() == 0.0                                          # q = prior -> KL = 0
    assert abs(kl_term(torch.ones(1, 1), torch.zeros(1, 1)).item() - 0.5) < 1e-6  # mu=1, sigma=1 -> 1/2
    lv = torch.full((1, 1), 2 * np.log(2.0))                                    # sigma = 2
    assert abs(kl_term(torch.zeros(1, 1), lv).item() - 0.5 * (4 - 1 - 2 * np.log(2))) < 1e-6
    x, p = torch.rand(5, 784), torch.rand(5, 784).clamp(0.01, 0.99)
    by_hand = -(x * p.log() + (1 - x) * (1 - p).log()).sum() / 5
    assert torch.allclose(recon_term(p, x), by_hand, rtol=1e-5)                 # BCE formula, summed over pixels
    mu, lv = torch.zeros(2, 3, requires_grad=True), torch.zeros(2, 3, requires_grad=True)
    VAE(3).reparameterize(mu, lv).sum().backward()
    assert mu.grad is not None and lv.grad is not None                          # gradients reach both heads
    model = VAE(16)
    assert sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) == 1_079_600
    assert tile(torch.arange(4 * 784.0).view(4, 784), 2, 2).shape == (56, 56)
    print("selfcheck ok")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    selfcheck()

docs.title: C — Train
docs.text:
Adam, learning rate \(10^{-3}\), batch size 128, 20 epochs. torch.manual_seed(42) is called inside train_vae() immediately before VAE(d), so it applies to every model; the training set is reshuffled every epoch with torch.randperm. Since 50 000 = 390 × 128 + 80, the last minibatch has 80 images and the running sums are weighted by the batch size, not by 128. For each epoch the function stores the two terms separately, on the training set (the average of the minibatch values over the epoch, while the weights are changing) and on the validation set (one pass in eval() mode with one sampled \(z\) per image, at the end of the epoch). All 20 epochs are in results_ex1.json; seven of them, in nats per image:

epoch train reconstruction train KL validation reconstruction validation KL 1 175.89 6.83 129.78 12.44 2 116.60 14.41 108.01 15.47 3 103.10 16.17 99.85 16.46 5 93.81 17.39 93.10 17.51 10 86.07 18.74 86.66 18.67 15 82.92 19.16 84.12 19.22 20 81.23 19.42 82.62 19.46

The validation KL is 12.44 nats at the first epoch and 19.46 nats at the last. The test set, evaluated once after the last epoch (again one sampled \(z\) per image):

reconstruction 81.97 nats + KL 19.49 nats = negative ELBO 101.46 nats per image.

The statement says a correct implementation lands around 81 nats of reconstruction and 20 nats of KL; this run gives 81.97 and 19.49. The test numbers sit next to the validation ones at epoch 20 (82.62 + 19.46 = 102.07; totals are computed from the unrounded terms): the test reconstruction is 0.65 nats lower, the KL differs by 0.03.

Reading Figure 1. Reconstruction (left): both curves fall steeply during the first three epochs (train 175.89 → 103.10, validation 129.78 → 99.85) and flatten afterwards. At epoch 20 the training value is 81.23 and the validation value 82.62, a gap of 1.39 nats, and the validation total decreases at every epoch, so there is no sign of overfitting. KL (right): both curves rise over the first epochs (validation 12.44 → 16.46 by epoch 3) and flatten after about epoch 10; the two curves overlap (19.42 and 19.46 at epoch 20). The validation KL is not strictly monotone: it peaks at 19.54 in epoch 18 and has small dips, such as 18.21 → 17.75 at epoch 7. Epoch 1 looks odd for a measurement reason, not a bug: the training curve is an average over the whole epoch, which starts from an untrained network (544.70 + 0.03 nats on the validation set), while the validation point is measured at the end of the epoch. That is why the epoch-1 training reconstruction (175.89) is above the validation one (129.78) and the training KL (6.83) below the validation KL (12.44).

docs.title: D — Reconstructions and samples
docs.text:
Figure 2. The top row is the first test image of each digit 0–9 (test indices 3, 2, 1, 18, 4, 8, 11, 0, 61, 7); the bottom row is model.decode(mu) for the same images, where mu is the encoder's mean: no \(z\) is sampled. Most digits keep their class, slant and thickness, and the strokes come back softer than they went in; the 5, the 8 and the 9 blur most (the 8 turns into a smudge, the 9 loses its tail, the 5 its sharp corners).

Figure 3. torch.manual_seed(0) is followed immediately by z = torch.randn(64, 16) (nothing else draws random numbers in between); the 64 codes are decoded and tiled \(8 \times 8\), rows and columns labelled 0–7.

Most of the samples are recognisable digits and all ten classes appear, but they are softer and more irregular than the reconstructions of Figure 2. By eye I count 6 of the 64 that are not a digit at all (row, column: (1, 0), (1, 1), (1, 5), (4, 0), (6, 2), (7, 2)) and about 9 more that can be read two ways. That is a visual count; another reader could differ by a few. Section 1E gives the two reasons.

"""Exercise 1 -- a VAE on MNIST (d = 16).

Trains the model, evaluates it once on the test set, and writes
    ../figures/fig1.png  fig2.png  fig3.png      the three figures of the exercise
    results_ex1.json                              every number quoted in the report
    data/vae_d16.pt                               checkpoint reused by Exercise 2 (gitignored)

Run from anywhere:  python ex1_vae_mnist.py      (about a minute on a laptop CPU)
"""
import json

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import torch

from vae import DATA_DIR, FIG_DIR, HERE, SEED, VAE, encode_all, evaluate, load_data, recon_term, tile, train_vae

D = 16
BLUE, ORANGE = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.grid": True, "grid.color": "#000000", "grid.alpha": 0.08,
                     "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "font.size": 10.5})


def figure1(hist):
    """Reconstruction x epoch and KL x epoch, each with the training and the validation curve."""
    epochs = [h["epoch"] for h in hist]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2))
    panels = [("rec", "Reconstruction term (BCE summed over 784 pixels)"),
              ("kl", f"KL term (closed form, summed over d = {D} dimensions)")]
    for ax, (key, title) in zip(axes, panels):
        ax.plot(epochs, [h[f"train_{key}"] for h in hist], "o-", ms=3.5, color=BLUE, label="train (average over the epoch)")
        ax.plot(epochs, [h[f"val_{key}"] for h in hist], "s--", ms=3.5, color=ORANGE, label="validation (end of the epoch)")
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10.5)
        ax.set_xlabel("epoch")
        ax.set_ylabel("nats per image")
        ax.set_xticks([1, 5, 10, 15, 20])
        ax.legend(frameon=False)
    # label the first and last validation KL; the first label sits right of the steep training curve, not on it
    for e, offset in ((0, (24, -6)), (-1, (4, -14))):
        v = hist[e]["val_kl"]
        axes[1].annotate(f"{v:.2f}", (hist[e]["epoch"], v), textcoords="offset points", xytext=offset, color=ORANGE)
    fig.suptitle("Figure 1 -- Training curves of the d = 16 VAE", fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig1.png", dpi=150)
    plt.close(fig)


def figure2(model, X_te, first):
    """First test image of each digit (top) and its reconstruction (bottom), decoded from mu."""
    with torch.no_grad():
        x = X_te[first]
        mu, _ = model.encode(x)
        # decode mu, do not sample z: mu is the centre of q(z|x), a fixed code per image. A sampled z adds
        # noise that says nothing about the image (the KL term is what pays for it) and changes at every run.
        recon = model.decode(mu)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.2))
    ax.imshow(tile(torch.cat([x, recon]), 2, 10).numpy(), cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    ax.grid(False)
    ax.set_xticks(14 + 28 * np.arange(10)); ax.set_xticklabels(range(10))
    ax.set_yticks([14, 42]); ax.set_yticklabels(["input", "reconstruction"])
    ax.set_xlabel("digit class"); ax.set_ylabel("row")
    ax.set_title("Figure 2 -- First test image of each digit and its reconstruction (decoding mu)", fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig2.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight", pad_inches=0.15)   # crop the blank band the 5:1 image leaves
    plt.close(fig)


def figure3(model):
    """8 x 8 images decoded from z ~ N(0, I), drawn right after torch.manual_seed(0)."""
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    z = torch.randn(64, D)                              # nothing else touches the RNG between seed and draw
    with torch.no_grad():
        samples = model.decode(z)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 7.6))
    ax.imshow(tile(samples, 8, 8).numpy(), cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    ax.grid(False)
    ticks = 14 + 28 * np.arange(8)
    ax.set_xticks(ticks); ax.set_xticklabels(range(8)); ax.set_yticks(ticks); ax.set_yticklabels(range(8))
    ax.set_xlabel("sample column"); ax.set_ylabel("sample row")
    ax.set_title(f"Figure 3 -- 64 images decoded from z ~ N(0, I), d = {D}, seed 0", fontweight="bold", fontsize=10.5)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig3.png", dpi=150)
    plt.close(fig)


@torch.no_grad()
def validation_diagnostics(model, data):
    """The numbers behind the 1E answers. Validation set only: the test set is kept for the headline numbers."""
    X_tr, X_va = data["X_train"], data["X_val"]
    mu_va, lv_va = encode_all(model, X_va)
    mu_tr, _ = encode_all(model, X_tr)
    out = {}

    # (a) which latent dimensions carry information
    kl_dim = (0.5 * (mu_va ** 2 + lv_va.exp() - 1 - lv_va)).mean(0)         # KL per dimension, nats
    active = (mu_va.var(0) > 0.01).nonzero().flatten()                       # mu varies across images
    out["kl_per_dim"] = kl_dim.tolist()
    out["active_units"] = len(active)
    out["mean_sigma_active"] = (0.5 * lv_va).exp()[:, active].mean().item()

    # (b) decode(mu) against decode(sampled z), same validation images
    torch.manual_seed(1)
    out["val_rec_sampled_z"] = evaluate(model, X_va)[0]
    out["val_rec_mu"] = recon_term(model.decode(mu_va), X_va).item()

    # (c) blur: pixel entropy of what the decoder outputs, sum_j H(p_j) = recon_term(p, p), nats per image
    torch.manual_seed(2)
    recon, prior = model.decode(mu_va), model.decode(torch.randn(10_000, D))
    gray = lambda p: ((p > 0.1) & (p < 0.9)).float().mean().item()           # share of "gray" pixels
    out["pixel_entropy"] = dict(data=recon_term(X_va, X_va).item(), recon_mu=recon_term(recon, recon).item(),
                                prior_samples=recon_term(prior, prior).item())
    out["gray_fraction"] = dict(data=gray(X_va), recon_mu=gray(recon), prior_samples=gray(prior))

    # (d) holes: distance of a code to the nearest encoded TRAINING image (active dimensions only).
    # If the aggregate posterior matched the prior, 5% of prior samples would exceed the 95th percentile
    # of the distances of codes drawn from the encoder itself.
    ref = mu_tr[:, active]
    torch.manual_seed(3)
    from_encoder = (mu_va + (0.5 * lv_va).exp() * torch.randn_like(mu_va))[:, active]
    from_prior = torch.randn(10_000, D)[:, active]
    nearest = lambda q: torch.cat([torch.cdist(q[i:i + 2000], ref).min(1).values for i in range(0, len(q), 2000)])
    d_enc, d_pri = nearest(from_encoder), nearest(from_prior)
    p95 = torch.quantile(d_enc, 0.95)
    out["holes"] = dict(median_encoder=d_enc.median().item(), median_prior=d_pri.median().item(),
                        p95_encoder=p95.item(), frac_prior_beyond_p95=(d_pri > p95).float().mean().item())

    # (e) two reference points for "why does the KL rise": the untrained network (same initialisation as the
    # trained one) and the best decoder that ignores z, a constant image (KL = 0 by construction). The
    # constant that minimises the summed BCE is the mean training image; the clamp only guards log(0).
    torch.manual_seed(SEED)
    untrained = VAE(D)
    torch.manual_seed(4)
    out["untrained_val"] = dict(zip(("rec", "kl"), evaluate(untrained, X_va)))
    mean_image = X_tr.mean(0).clamp(1e-4, 1 - 1e-4)
    out["mean_image_val_rec"] = recon_term(mean_image.expand_as(X_va), X_va).item()
    return out


def main():
    FIG_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    DATA_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

    # A -- data. Train and validation feed the training loop; the test set is not touched until below.
    data = load_data()
    print(f"split: train {len(data['X_train'])}, validation {len(data['X_val'])}, test {len(data['X_test'])}")

    # B + C -- build (torch.manual_seed(42) inside train_vae) and train for 20 epochs
    model, hist = train_vae(D, data["X_train"], data["X_val"])
    torch.save(model.state_dict(), DATA_DIR / "vae_d16.pt")
    n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())

    # --- the test set is used for the first time here: final numbers and figures only ---
    X_te, y_te = data["X_test"], data["y_test"]
    test_rec, test_kl = evaluate(model, X_te)
    print(f"TEST d={D}: reconstruction {test_rec:.2f}  KL {test_kl:.2f}  negative ELBO {test_rec + test_kl:.2f}  ({n_params} parameters)")
    print(f"validation KL: epoch 1 = {hist[0]['val_kl']:.2f}, epoch 20 = {hist[-1]['val_kl']:.2f}")

    first = [int((y_te == k).nonzero()[0]) for k in range(10)]               # first test image of each digit
    figure1(hist)
    figure2(model, X_te, first)
    figure3(model)

    diag = validation_diagnostics(model, data)
    print(json.dumps(diag, indent=1))

    # the numbers are bit-exact only for this torch build and thread count (see the report): record them
    results = dict(env=dict(torch=torch.__version__, threads=torch.get_num_threads()),
                   split=dict(train=50_000, val=10_000, test=10_000), n_params=n_params, history=hist,
                   test=dict(rec=test_rec, kl=test_kl, neg_elbo=test_rec + test_kl),
                   val_kl_first=hist[0]["val_kl"], val_kl_last=hist[-1]["val_kl"],
                   first_test_index_per_digit=first, diagnostics=diag)
    (HERE / "results_ex1.json").write_text(json.dumps(results, indent=1))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: E — Analysis
docs.text:
The numbers below come from results_ex1.json: the per-epoch history and validation_diagnostics(), which uses the validation set only, with its own fixed seeds, after the figures are made.

(1) The KL rises during the first epochs while the total falls. Why would the optimizer pay more KL? Because the loss is the sum of the two terms and the KL is the price of the information the code carries. At initialisation the encoder is almost the prior (untrained network on the validation set: KL 0.03, reconstruction 544.70), so \(z\) says nothing about \(x\), and a decoder that ignores \(z\) can at best output one constant image, the mean training image: 205.60 nats of reconstruction at KL \(= 0\). The reconstruction can only fall below that if \(z\) tells the decoder something about the input, and information about \(x\) in the code is exactly what the KL measures: the average KL equals the mutual information between image and code plus the distance of the aggregate posterior to the prior, so it is at least that information, and the \(d = 16\) code carries at most 19.5 nats (28.1 bits). The optimiser therefore pays one more nat of KL whenever that buys more than one nat of reconstruction, and early on it buys far more. From epoch 1 to epoch 20 the validation KL rises by 7.02 nats (12.44 → 19.46) while the validation reconstruction falls by 47.16 nats (129.78 → 82.62): about 6.7 nats of reconstruction per nat of KL, and the total falls by 40.14 (142.21 → 102.07). The rise of the KL is the model starting to use its code, not a failure. The curve flattens as the exchange rate drops (7.2 nats of reconstruction per nat of KL between epochs 1 and 2, 5.1 between epochs 10 and 20), but it is still above 1 after 20 epochs, so training has not reached the point where one more nat of KL stops paying. The same trade-off decides which dimensions are used: 11 of the 16 latent dimensions carry between 0.95 and 2.53 nats each, and 5 stay at the prior (KL below 0.002 each), because for them the information would cost more than it buys.

(2) Figure 3 looks worse than Figure 2. Two separate reasons.

Where the prior samples land (the encoder side). The decoder was trained on codes drawn from the clouds \(q(z \mid x)\) of the training images, and the union of those clouds, the aggregate posterior, does not fill the prior \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\). Each cloud is small (mean \(\sigma = 0.20\) over the 11 active dimensions, against 1 for the prior) and the model only pays 19.5 nats of KL, so there are gaps between the clouds; a prior sample that lands in a gap is an input the decoder never saw, and it returns a hybrid or a non-digit. Measured on the validation set (distance, in the active dimensions, from a code to the nearest encoded training mean): the median is 1.16 for codes drawn from the encoder itself and 1.49 for prior samples, and 32.3 % of the prior samples are farther than the 95th percentile of the encoder's own codes (1.64), where 5 % would be expected if the aggregate posterior matched the prior. This fits what Figure 3 shows: 6 non-digits and about 9 ambiguous images in my visual count.

What the decoder outputs for a given \(z\) (the decoder side, independent of the first reason). The decoder returns the Bernoulli mean \(E[x \mid z]\), a probability for every pixel, not a sample from it. Different images have overlapping posteriors around the same \(z\), and the BCE-optimal output for them is their average: gray strokes and soft edges. This holds even for the best possible code (the reconstructions of Figure 2 are already soft), so it is not a bug, and it would be there even if every prior sample landed on a well-trained code. Measured as the summed pixel entropy of the output (validation set, nats per image): real images 45.66 (this is also the floor of the BCE, \(\mathrm{BCE}(x, x)\)), reconstructions \(\mathrm{decode}(\mu)\) 81.15, prior samples 91.45. The share of gray pixels (\(0.1 < p < 0.9\)) is 8.6 %, 14.9 % and 17.0 %. The jump from data to reconstructions (+35.50 nats) is mostly the second reason, since \(\mu\) is the best code the model has for those images; the further +10.30 from reconstructions to prior samples is where the first reason adds on top.

(3) Why decode \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and not a sampled \(z\) in Figure 2? Figure 2 asks what the model can reconstruct. \(\mu\) is the centre of \(q(z \mid x)\) (its mean and its mode): one deterministic code per image, the same on every run. A sampled \(z = \mu + \sigma \odot \varepsilon\) adds noise that carries no information about the image (the KL term is what pays for allowing it) and draws a different picture each time, so a sampled row would mix the quality of the model with the luck of \(\varepsilon\). It also costs quality: on the validation set the BCE of \(\mathrm{decode}(\mu)\) is 77.54 nats against 82.64 with one sampled \(z\) per image, so sampling adds 5.10 nats (6.6 %) at the typical perturbation \(\sigma = 0.20\) per active dimension. The loss and ELBO numbers of 1C still use a sampled \(z\), because the ELBO is an expectation under \(q(z \mid x)\); reporting the \(\mathrm{decode}(\mu)\) value as the reconstruction term would give about 77.5 instead of about 82 and flatter the model.

docs.text: A latent space you can see.

docs.title: A — Train a 2-D VAE
docs.text:
The same train_vae() call with d = 2: same data and split, torch.manual_seed(42) right before the model is built, \(\beta = 1\), Adam with learning rate \(10^{-3}\), batch size 128, 20 epochs. Only \(d\) changes (the two heads and the first decoder layer shrink: 1 068 820 parameters instead of 1 079 600). Test set, one sampled \(z\) per image, nats per image; the \(d = 16\) row is read from results_ex1.json, so both rows come from the same evaluation.

reconstruction KL negative ELBO \(d = 16\) (Exercise 1) 81.97 19.49 101.46 \(d = 2\) 135.12 6.57 141.69 difference (\(d = 2\) minus \(d = 16\)) +53.16 −12.93 +40.23

The 2-D model reaches a test reconstruction of 135.12 nats and a test KL of 6.57 nats (negative ELBO 141.69), as the statement expects (roughly 135 and 7). Compared with \(d = 16\) it pays 12.93 nats less KL and 53.16 nats more reconstruction error. Its validation KL is 5.09 at the first epoch and 6.56 at the last.

docs.title: B — The encoded test set
docs.text: Figure 4 shows 10 000 points: every test image (the script asserts it), at its encoder mean \(\mu\), no sampling, one colour per digit, with the ten digits in the legend. The dashed square is the region decoded in Figure 5. The classes fan out around the origin: 0 far to the left, 1 to the right, 7 on top, 3 at the bottom, 6, 2, 8 and 5 packed in the centre, and 4 and 9 lying on top of each other right of the centre. The codes use the plane the way the prior wants, at the prior's scale (variance of \(\mu\) 1.19 and 1.01 along the two axes), while each individual posterior is tiny (mean \(\sigma\) 0.045 and 0.047).

docs.title: C — The decoded plane
docs.text:
I decode a \(15 \times 15\) grid with \(z = \Phi^{-1}(q)\), \(q\) running over 15 evenly spaced values in \([0.05, 0.95]\) (scipy.stats.norm.ppf), which gives \(z \in \{-1.645, -1.204, -0.921, -0.697, -0.504, -0.328, -0.162, 0, 0.162, 0.328, 0.504, 0.697, 0.921, 1.204, 1.645\}\) on both axes. The 225 codes are \([z_1, z_2]\); the layout is Figure 4's: \(z_1\) increases from left to right and \(z_2\) from bottom to top (the first printed row is the largest \(z_2\)), and every image is drawn on the same gray scale \([0, 1]\).

Why this spacing gives every cell the same prior mass: \(\Phi\) is the CDF of the prior along each axis, so evenly spaced \(q\) means evenly spaced cumulative probability, and each of the 14 gaps between neighbouring grid values holds the same \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) mass \(\Delta q = 0.9 / 14 = 0.0643\); the two coordinates being independent, every grid rectangle holds \(\Delta q^2 = 0.0041\) of the prior (the inner \(14 \times 14\) block holds \(0.9^2 = 0.81\)), where a linear grid would spend most of its cells in the thin tails.

Figure 5 has Figure 4's layout: 0 on the left, 1 on the right, 7 at the top right, 3 and 5 at the bottom, 6 left of the centre. The grid covers the central 90 % of the prior along each axis, so the far tails of the 0, 3 and 7 clouds (beyond \(\pm 1.645\)) are outside it. Section 2E reads it in detail.

docs.title: D — Interpolation
docs.text:
The two test images are test image 8 (a 5) and test image 0 (a 7). I did not pick them by eye: among the 45 pairs of different digits that can be formed from the ten images of Figure 2, they are the pair with the largest gap, in the committed run, between the pixel row and the latent row in their distance to real digits, where "distance to real digits" is the L2 distance, in pixel space, from an image to the closest of the 10 000 validation images, averaged over the 8 interior images (\(0 < t < 1\)). That is the most favourable pair for the latent row, so 2E also reports the average over all 45 pairs. The pair is fixed in the script (IA, IB = 8, 0); the computation over the 45 pairs is only printed and saved in results_ex2.json as a diagnostic, because its argmax moves with float rounding (see the note on reproducibility at the top: REPLACE_PAIR_8T).

Figure 6 uses \(t\) = torch.linspace(0, 1, 10), ten columns including both ends. Top row, in pixel space: \((1 - t)\,\mathbf{x}_a + t\,\mathbf{x}_b\) on the original test images. Bottom row, in latent space, with the \(d = 16\) model of Exercise 1 (the checkpoint it saves): decode((1 - t) * mu_a + t * mu_b), with the encoder means \(\mu_a, \mu_b\) of the two images. The end images of the bottom row are therefore reconstructions of \(\mathbf{x}_a\) and \(\mathbf{x}_b\), not the originals (compare with Figure 2).

"""Exercise 2 -- a latent space you can see (d = 2), and interpolation with the d = 16 model.

Trains the d = 2 VAE (same code, data, seed, beta and budget as Exercise 1) and reuses the d = 16
model of Exercise 1 (data/vae_d16.pt; Exercise 1 is run first if the checkpoint is missing). Writes
    ../figures/fig4.png  fig5.png  fig6.png
    results_ex2.json                              every number quoted in the report

Run from anywhere:  python ex2_latent_plane.py   (about a minute on a laptop CPU)
"""
import itertools
import json

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import torch
from scipy.stats import norm
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

from vae import DATA_DIR, FIG_DIR, HERE, VAE, encode_all, evaluate, load_data, tile, train_vae

plt.rcParams.update({"axes.grid": True, "grid.color": "#000000", "grid.alpha": 0.08,
                     "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "font.size": 10.5})

# 15 evenly spaced quantiles of the prior, mapped back to z: equal prior mass per step along each axis
Q = np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 15)
ZG = norm.ppf(Q) + 0.0                                    # -1.645 ... +1.645, denser near 0
fmt = lambda v: f"{v:.2f}".replace("-0.00", "0.00")

# Figure 6 pair, PINNED: test image 8 (a 5) and test image 0 (a 7), two of the ten images of Figure 2. In the committed
# run it is also the pair with the largest gap computed in main(), but that argmax is float-sensitive (another thread
# count picks another pair), so the script prints the diagnostic and does not let it move Figure 6.
IA, IB = 8, 0


def figure4(mu, y):
    """Scatter of mu for all 10 000 test images, colored by digit."""
    assert len(mu) == len(y) == 10_000                    # every test image, no subsampling
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.2, 6.2))
    for k in range(10):
        m = (y == k)
        ax.scatter(mu[m, 0], mu[m, 1], s=5, alpha=0.6, linewidths=0, color=plt.get_cmap("tab10")(k), label=str(k))
    lo, hi = ZG[0], ZG[-1]                                # the square decoded in Figure 5
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((lo, lo), hi - lo, hi - lo, fill=False, ls="--", lw=1, ec="black"))
    ax.text(hi, lo - 0.06, "Figure 5 grid", ha="right", va="top", fontsize=8.5,    # a label, not an 11th legend entry
            bbox=dict(fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85, pad=1.5))
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$\mu_1$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\mu_2$")
    ax.set_title("Figure 4 -- Encoded test set, d = 2 (10 000 images, colored by digit)", fontweight="bold")
    ax.legend(title="digit", markerscale=3, loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 0.5), frameon=False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig4.png", dpi=150)
    plt.close(fig)


def figure5(m2):
    """15 x 15 decoded plane. Columns: z1 increasing to the right; rows: z2 increasing UPWARD (as in Figure 4)."""
    Z = torch.tensor([[z1, z2] for z2 in ZG[::-1] for z1 in ZG], dtype=torch.float32)     # row-major, top row first
    with torch.no_grad():
        imgs = m2.decode(Z)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 8.6))
    ax.imshow(tile(imgs, 15, 15).numpy(), cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    ax.grid(False)
    ticks = 14 + 28 * np.arange(15)
    ax.set_xticks(ticks); ax.set_xticklabels([fmt(v) for v in ZG], rotation=90, fontsize=7.5)
    ax.set_yticks(ticks); ax.set_yticklabels([fmt(v) for v in ZG[::-1]], fontsize=7.5)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$z_1 = \Phi^{-1}(q)$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$z_2 = \Phi^{-1}(q)$")
    # cell index 1-15 (column from the left, row from the top) on the top and right axes: the addresses the report uses
    top, right = ax.secondary_xaxis("top"), ax.secondary_yaxis("right")
    top.set_xticks(ticks); top.set_xticklabels(range(1, 16), fontsize=7.5); top.set_xlabel("column", fontsize=8.5)
    right.set_yticks(ticks); right.set_yticklabels(range(1, 16), fontsize=7.5); right.set_ylabel("row", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_title("Figure 5 -- Decoded 15 x 15 latent plane, d = 2 (q evenly spaced in [0.05, 0.95])", fontweight="bold", fontsize=10)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig5.png", dpi=150)
    plt.close(fig)


def rows(m16, X_te, ia, ib, t):
    """Pixel-space row and latent-space row (d = 16 model, decoding the interpolated mu) for the pair (ia, ib)."""
    pix = (1 - t) * X_te[ia] + t * X_te[ib]
    with torch.no_grad():
        mu, _ = m16.encode(X_te[[ia, ib]])
        lat = m16.decode((1 - t) * mu[0] + t * mu[1])
    return pix, lat


def figure6(pix, lat, ia, ib, ya, yb, t):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.2))
    ax.imshow(tile(torch.cat([pix, lat]), 2, 10).numpy(), cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    ax.grid(False)
    ax.set_xticks(14 + 28 * np.arange(10)); ax.set_xticklabels([f"{v:.2f}" for v in t.flatten()])
    ax.set_yticks([14, 42]); ax.set_yticklabels(["pixel space", "latent space (d = 16)"])
    ax.set_xlabel("t"); ax.set_ylabel("interpolation")
    ax.set_title(f"Figure 6 -- Interpolation from test image {ia} (digit {ya}) to test image {ib} (digit {yb})", fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fig6.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight", pad_inches=0.15)   # crop the blank band the 5:1 image leaves
    plt.close(fig)


def main():
    FIG_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    data = load_data()
    X_tr, y_tr, X_va, X_te, y_te = data["X_train"], data["y_train"], data["X_val"], data["X_test"], data["y_test"]

    # the d = 16 model of Exercise 1 (checkpoint written by ex1_vae_mnist.py) and its test numbers
    ckpt = DATA_DIR / "vae_d16.pt"
    if not ckpt.exists():
        import ex1_vae_mnist
        ex1_vae_mnist.main()
    m16 = VAE(16)
    m16.load_state_dict(torch.load(ckpt))
    m16.eval()
    ex1 = json.loads((HERE / "results_ex1.json").read_text())["test"]

    # A -- the 2-D model: nothing changes except d
    m2, hist2 = train_vae(2, X_tr, X_va)
    rec2, kl2 = evaluate(m2, X_te)                        # test set: final numbers only from here on
    print(f"TEST d=2 : reconstruction {rec2:.2f}  KL {kl2:.2f}  negative ELBO {rec2 + kl2:.2f}")
    print(f"TEST d=16: reconstruction {ex1['rec']:.2f}  KL {ex1['kl']:.2f}  negative ELBO {ex1['neg_elbo']:.2f}   (from Exercise 1)")
    per_digit = {k: dict(d16=evaluate(m16, X_te[y_te == k])[0], d2=evaluate(m2, X_te[y_te == k])[0]) for k in range(10)}

    # B -- encoded test set
    mu_te, lv_te = encode_all(m2, X_te)
    mu_tr, _ = encode_all(m2, X_tr)
    figure4(mu_te.numpy(), y_te.numpy())
    cent = np.stack([mu_te[y_te == k].mean(0).numpy() for k in range(10)])             # digit centroids in the plane

    # overlap, measured: 15-nearest-neighbour vote in the 2-D code (fit on the training codes)
    pred2 = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=15).fit(mu_tr.numpy(), y_tr.numpy()).predict(mu_te.numpy())
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_te.numpy(), pred2)
    mu16_te, _ = encode_all(m16, X_te)
    mu16_tr, _ = encode_all(m16, X_tr)
    pred16 = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=15).fit(mu16_tr.numpy(), y_tr.numpy()).predict(mu16_te.numpy())
    cm16 = confusion_matrix(y_te.numpy(), pred16)
    cell = lambda p: (14 - int(np.abs(ZG - p[1]).argmin()) + 1, int(np.abs(ZG - p[0]).argmin()) + 1)   # 1-based (row from top, col from left)
    top = sorted(((int(cm[a, b] + cm[b, a]), a, b) for a, b in itertools.combinations(range(10), 2)), reverse=True)[:5]
    overlap = [dict(pair=[a, b], confused=tot, rate_a_as_b=float(cm[a, b] / cm[a].sum()), rate_b_as_a=float(cm[b, a] / cm[b].sum()),
                    centroid_distance=float(np.linalg.norm(cent[a] - cent[b])), midpoint=((cent[a] + cent[b]) / 2).tolist(),
                    figure5_cell_row_col=cell((cent[a] + cent[b]) / 2)) for tot, a, b in top]

    # C -- decoded plane
    figure5(m2)
    dq = float(Q[1] - Q[0])

    # D -- interpolation between the pinned pair (IA, IB), two different digits. The gap diagnostic is computed for the
    # 45 pairs of Figure 2's images (first test image of each digit): how much farther from real digits the in-between
    # pixel images are than the latent ones. It is only reported, never used to pick the pair.
    first = json.loads((HERE / "results_ex1.json").read_text())["first_test_index_per_digit"]
    t = torch.linspace(0, 1, 10)[:, None]
    nearest = lambda imgs: torch.cat([torch.cdist(imgs[i:i + 1000], X_va).min(1).values
                                      for i in range(0, len(imgs), 1000)]).mean().item()   # mean L2 distance to the closest validation image
    gaps = {}                                             # (test index a, test index b) -> (gap, pixel row, latent row)
    for a, b in itertools.combinations(range(10), 2):
        pix, lat = rows(m16, X_te, first[a], first[b], t)
        dp, dl = nearest(pix[1:-1]), nearest(lat[1:-1])
        gaps[first[a], first[b]] = (dp - dl, dp, dl)
    best = max(gaps, key=lambda k: gaps[k][0])            # the pair this run's model would pick
    gap, d_pix, d_lat = gaps[IA, IB]                      # (KeyError unless IA, IB are two of Figure 2's images, a < b)
    ia, ib, a, b = IA, IB, int(y_te[IA]), int(y_te[IB])
    assert a != b                                         # two different digits (the statement)
    print(f"Figure 6 pair (pinned): test {ia} (digit {a}) -> test {ib} (digit {b}), gap {gap:.2f}; "
          f"largest gap of this run: test {best[0]} -> test {best[1]}, gap {gaps[best][0]:.2f}"
          + ("" if best == (IA, IB) else "   <-- differs from the pinned pair (float-sensitive argmax)"))
    pix, lat = rows(m16, X_te, ia, ib, t)
    figure6(pix, lat, ia, ib, a, b, t)

    # Scale for those distances, same reference set (validation images): a real test digit, and the t = 0.5 image
    # of 500 random pairs of test images of different digits (pixel blend vs decoded latent midpoint, d = 16).
    pa, pb = torch.randint(0, len(X_te), (2, 1000), generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))
    ok = y_te[pa] != y_te[pb]
    pa, pb = pa[ok][:500], pb[ok][:500]
    with torch.no_grad():
        mid_lat = m16.decode(0.5 * (m16.encode(X_te[pa])[0] + m16.encode(X_te[pb])[0]))
    scale = dict(real_test_digit=nearest(X_te), pixel_blend_t05=nearest(0.5 * (X_te[pa] + X_te[pb])),
                 latent_midpoint=nearest(mid_lat), n_random_pairs=len(pa))

    results = dict(
        env=dict(torch=torch.__version__, threads=torch.get_num_threads()),   # bit-exact only for this build and thread count
        d2=dict(history=hist2, n_params=sum(p.numel() for p in m2.parameters()), test=dict(rec=rec2, kl=kl2, neg_elbo=rec2 + kl2),
                val_kl_first=hist2[0]["val_kl"], val_kl_last=hist2[-1]["val_kl"],
                mu_var=mu_te.var(0).tolist(), mean_sigma=(0.5 * lv_te).exp().mean(0).tolist(),
                mu_range=[mu_te.min(0).values.tolist(), mu_te.max(0).values.tolist()]),
        d16_test=ex1,
        diff_d2_minus_d16=dict(rec=rec2 - ex1["rec"], kl=kl2 - ex1["kl"], neg_elbo=rec2 + kl2 - ex1["neg_elbo"]),
        kl_bits=dict(d16=ex1["kl"] / np.log(2), d2=kl2 / np.log(2), class_label=np.log2(10)),   # nats -> bits
        per_digit_test_rec=per_digit,
        knn15_test_accuracy=dict(d2=float((pred2 == y_te.numpy()).mean()), d16=float((pred16 == y_te.numpy()).mean())),
        knn15_recall_per_digit=dict(d2=(cm.diagonal() / cm.sum(1)).tolist(), d16=(cm16.diagonal() / cm16.sum(1)).tolist()),
        centroids=cent.tolist(), overlap_top5=overlap,
        grid=dict(z=ZG.tolist(), q=Q.tolist(), dq=dq, mass_per_cell=dq ** 2, inner_mass=(14 * dq) ** 2),
        interpolation=dict(index_a=ia, digit_a=a, index_b=ib, digit_b=b, t=t.flatten().tolist(),
                           nn_dist_pixel_row=d_pix, nn_dist_latent_row=d_lat, gap=gap,
                           largest_gap_pair_this_run=dict(index_a=best[0], index_b=best[1], gap=gaps[best][0]),
                           mean_gap_all_45_pairs=float(np.mean([g[0] for g in gaps.values()])),
                           min_gap=min(g[0] for g in gaps.values()), max_gap=max(g[0] for g in gaps.values()),
                           n_pairs_latent_closer=sum(g[0] > 0 for g in gaps.values()), scale=scale))
    (HERE / "results_ex2.json").write_text(json.dumps(results, indent=1))
    print(json.dumps({k: v for k, v in results.items() if k not in ("d2",)}, indent=1))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: E — Analysis
docs.text:
(1) Which digits overlap in Figure 4? The same transition in Figure 5. The strongest overlap is 4 with 9: the purple and cyan clouds lie on top of each other right of the centre, and their centroids are only 0.10 apart ((0.18, 0.59) and (0.28, 0.56); the prior has \(\sigma = 1\)). To measure it rather than judge by eye, I fitted a 15-nearest-neighbour vote on the 2-D codes of the training images and applied it to the test codes. It labels 27.6 % of the test 4s as 9 and 31.3 % of the test 9s as 4: 587 test images in the two directions. Then come 3 with 5 (9.1 % of the 3s labelled 5, 28.7 % of the 5s labelled 3; 348 images), 3 with 8 (180), 5 with 8 (155) and 7 with 9 (121). The 0s (far left) and the 1s (right) are almost isolated (vote recall 97.3 % and 97.7 %), while 5, 9 and 4 are the worst recognised (55.9 %, 60.9 % and 67.6 %). Over all digits the vote is right for 80.38 % of the test images, against 96.02 % with the \(d = 16\) codes.

In Figure 5 (rows and columns counted from 1 at the top-left) the same transitions are:

  • 4 and 9. The 4s, with an open top, form a diagonal band from (3, 5) down to (5, 9) and the 9s, with a closed loop, lie to its right and above it (columns 10–12 of rows 4–8). The midpoint of the two centroids falls at row 5, column 9, the last 4-like cell before the first 9 of that row. Cell (4, 9) is a blurry hybrid, a 4 whose top bar has closed into a flat-topped loop, between the 4 at (4, 8) and the 9 at (4, 10). Around rows 6–7, columns 5–9, the cells are blotchy smudges where 6, 2, 4, 8 and 9 meet and none of them is readable.
  • 3, 5 and 8. At the bottom, rows 13–15, a narrow band of 3s (columns 6–8 in rows 13–14, widening to columns 7–10 in row 15) sits between 5s on both sides. The 3–5 midpoint is (14, 7), inside the band, and the cells at its edges, (14, 6) and (14, 8), are 5/3 hybrids. The 8s lie directly above the 3s (rows 11–12); the 3–8 midpoint is (13, 7), a 3, and (13, 4) to (13, 6) are 8/3 hybrids, an 8 whose upper loop weakens as it turns into that 3. The 5–8 midpoint is (12, 8), an 8 whose upper right is opening into the 5 at (12, 9).
  • 7 and 9. At the top, the midpoint is (2, 10), a 7. In row 2 the 9 at (2, 8) becomes a 9 with an opening loop at (2, 9) and a 7 at (2, 10): the loop dissolves into the 7's top bar.

Most of these changes are gradual, a stroke closing or a loop opening, with a blurry hybrid in between and no third shape. Not all of them: from the 4 at (3, 6) to the 9 at (3, 7), and from the 3 at (13, 7) to the 5 at (13, 8), the shape switches within one grid step with no hybrid between.

(2) \(d = 2\) reconstructs clearly worse than \(d = 16\). What do two numbers per image force the model to throw away? Nearly everything except the class and a coarse style. The cost is test reconstruction 135.12 against 81.97 (+53.16 nats, +65 %), KL 6.57 against 19.49 (−12.93) and negative ELBO 141.69 against 101.46 (+40.23). In bits, the code carries at most 9.5 bits (the KL upper-bounds the information the code holds about the image) against 28.1 for \(d = 16\), and merely naming one of ten digits takes \(\log_2 10 = 3.3\) bits. Even a code that named the digit perfectly would keep at most 6.2 bits (4.26 nats) for everything else, and this one does not name it reliably (15-NN accuracy 80.38 % against 96.02 %): the classes must share the plane and overlap (Figure 4). It is a capacity limit, not noise: both dimensions are used (variance of \(\mu\) 1.19 and 1.01) and the posteriors are narrow (mean \(\sigma\) 0.045 and 0.047, against 0.20 over the active dimensions of \(d = 16\)).

Figure 5 shows what is lost. All 225 decoded images are smooth, blurry prototypes of their digit with a similar medium stroke thickness and no writer-specific detail (no hooks, crossbars or loop variants), and inside a digit's region the picture changes along one or two smooth directions only. The 1s along the right edge, for example, differ only in slant: they lean left in rows 5–6, stand upright in rows 7–8 and lean further and further right from row 9 down to row 15. The penalty also follows how much the digit varies, in test reconstruction nats for \(d = 16 \to d = 2\): digit 1, almost a one-parameter family, goes from 39.5 to 51.8 (+12.3, the smallest), while 2 (97.9 → 169.6, +71.7, the largest), 3 (+65.6) and 5 (+63.7), whose shapes vary most, pay the most.

(3) Compare the two rows of Figure 6. Which one passes through images that look like digits, and why does the other one not? The latent row does; the pixel row does not. The pixel row is a cross-fade: at \(t = 0.44\) and \(0.56\) the 5 and the 7 are both on the image at about half intensity, the 5's bowl and the 7's stem drawn on top of each other, so no image between the two ends is a digit. Every image of the latent row is one connected glyph: for \(t = 0\) to \(0.22\) a blurry 5/8-like shape (the reconstruction of the 5, not the 5 itself), at \(t = 0.33\) and \(0.44\) a 9-like loop on a stem, at \(t = 0.56\) a 7 with a faint remnant of that loop, and from \(t = 0.67\) a clean 7.

The reason is geometry. Digit images lie on a thin, curved set inside the 784-dimensional pixel space, and the pixel average of two points of such a set is generally off it: a superposition of two digits is not a digit. The latent space is different on both ends: the KL term keeps the clouds of different images overlapping and centred on the origin, so the straight segment from \(\mu_a\) to \(\mu_b\) mostly runs through regions where the decoder has seen data, and the nonlinear decoder maps that straight segment onto a curve along the image set. In numbers (L2 distance from the 8 interior images to the closest of the 10 000 validation images, averaged): 5.42 for the pixel row against 4.07 for the latent row for this pair, and the latent row is the closer one for all 45 pairs of Figure 2's images (mean difference 0.75, from 0.02 to 1.35; this pair has the largest). For scale, a real test digit is 4.72 from its closest validation digit, and for 500 random pairs of different digits the \(t = 0.5\) image is 5.47 away in pixel space and 4.52 in latent space. The caveat is that L2 rewards blur (a blurry image is close to many digits), so these numbers understate the visual gap; the pictures are the stronger evidence.

docs.title: Project — Will this station flood tomorrow?
docs.text: One question, asked 456,600 times: given everything a river monitoring station has recorded up to today, will it report a flood tomorrow?

docs.title: Team
docs.text:
• Luigi Lopes
  • Lucas Abatepietro
  • Marcelo Alonso

docs.title: The dataset
docs.text:
Kaggle, ASIA-FLOOD: 25-Year Flood Risk Atlas (2000–2024) by aliahmadmphil, CC BY-SA 4.0. Three tables:

file rows what it holds station_daily_data_full.csv 456,600 one row per station per day: 50 stations × 9,132 days, 2000-01-01 to 2024-12-31 vulnerability_data.csv 10 one row per river basin: area, population, poverty rate, hospitals, resilience scores asia_flood_geospatial.geojson 10 one Polygon per river basin, with area, population, risk and vulnerability labels (station coordinates live in the daily table, as latitude/longitude)

The daily table has 4 measured variables (rainfall_mm, river_level_m, soil_moisture_percent, temperature_celsius), calendar fields (date, season, monsoon_season, day_of_year), identifiers (station_id, basin, country, latitude, longitude), a data_quality_score, and three outcome columns: flood_event_occurred (0/1), severity_level, flood_risk_score.

The data is kept out of git (docs/projects/data/, gitignored) and out of the built site. The scripts download or expect it there.

This dataset is synthetic

Its README says it was generated (2026-07-23). Some station names do not match their coordinates (a "Luang Prabang" at 16.1°N 103.0°E, which is Thailand, not Laos), and, as shown below, floods occur only during the monsoon flag. Every method here is real; the numbers describe a simulator, not Asia. Nothing in this project is a claim about actual flood risk.

docs.title: What a first pass over the data says
docs.text:
These numbers shape every decision that follows. They come from station_daily_data_full.csv before any modelling.

  • The panel is complete: every station has all 9,132 days, no duplicates, no missing values.
  • 2.17 % of station-days are floods (9,889 of 456,600). This is an imbalanced problem; accuracy is meaningless (predicting "no flood" scores 97.8 %).
  • Two columns are the target in disguise. severity_level == "Extreme" coincides with flood_event_occurred == 1 on 9,889 of 9,921 rows, and flood_risk_score > 7 separates the same-day event perfectly (ROC-AUC 1.000). They are outputs of whatever generated the floods, not measurements. They are excluded from the features. flood_risk_score appears once, as a reference baseline, labelled as such.
  • Floods happen only in monsoon season. The flood rate is 5.17 % when monsoon_season = 1 and exactly 0 % otherwise. A rule that says "never outside the monsoon" is therefore a baseline every model has to beat inside the monsoon, where the actual problem lives.
  • Floods are isolated days, not episodes. P(flood tomorrow | flood today) = 7.6 %, against a 2.17 % base rate. Yesterday's label helps a little; it will not carry a model.
  • Today's measurements carry real signal for tomorrow. Used alone, each gives ROC-AUC for the next-day event of: soil moisture 0.836, rainfall 0.809, temperature 0.796, river level 0.795. The modelling bet is that windows over the past days (accumulated rain, rising river) do better than any single day.
  • Events per year are stable (354–439), so a chronological split is fair to both ends.

docs.title: The task, precisely
docs.text: For station \(s\) and day \(t\), predict \(y_{s,t+1} = \) flood_event_occurred on day \(t+1\), using only rows of station \(s\) with date \(\le t\) plus static basin information. The prediction is a probability; the operating threshold is chosen on validation data for a stated recall target, because a flood warning system is judged on the floods it misses.

docs.title: Rules that stop leakage
docs.text:
1. No same-day outcome columns as inputs. flood_event_occurred, severity_level and flood_risk_score for day \(t\) never enter the feature vector for \(y_{t+1}\). (flood_event_occurred for days \(\le t\) may enter as an explicit lag feature; it is what a real system would know.)
  2. Every feature is computed from the past only. Rolling windows end at day \(t\). Shifts are checked by construction: a test asserts that permuting the future leaves every feature unchanged.
  3. Chronological split, by date, same dates for every station: train 2000–2016 (17 years), validation 2017–2020 (4), test 2021–2024 (4). No random shuffling: rows one day apart are near-duplicates, and a random split would leak.
  4. Every statistic is fitted on train only: scalers, per-station means and standard deviations, category vocabularies, the decision threshold.
  5. The test split is touched once, at the end, with the model and threshold frozen.

docs.title: Phase 1 — EDA (projects/eda/)
docs.text:
Deliverables, each with a figure and the numbers in the text:

  1. Panel completeness and the class balance above, per station and per year.
  2. Distributions of the four measurements, raw and log-transformed where skewed (rainfall).
  3. Seasonality: flood rate by month and by day_of_year; the monsoon gate, shown plainly.
  4. What a flood looks like: the mean trajectory of each measurement over the 14 days before and after a flood, against the station's normal. This picture decides the window lengths.
  5. Between-station differences: flood rate, mean river level and rainfall per station and basin; whether the vulnerability table explains any of it.
  6. Correlations among measurements and with the next-day target.
  7. The leakage audit: the two outcome-derived columns, with the numbers that prove it.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Feature engineering and normalisation
docs.text:
Built by one function that takes a station's day-ordered frame and returns features aligned to \(t\), so it is the same code for train, validation, test and any future day.

group features why today the 4 measurements at \(t\) the strongest single-day signal (AUC ≈ 0.8 each) lags each measurement at \(t-1, t-2, t-3\) the direction things are moving windows rainfall sum over 3, 7, 14, 30 days; river level mean and max over 3, 7, 14 days; soil moisture mean over 3, 7 days floods follow accumulated rain and a rising river, not one wet day changes day-over-day change of river level and soil moisture; 7-day slope of river level rising versus falling anomalies each measurement as a z-score against that station's training mean and sd "unusually high for here" is what matters, and it is what a station operator would say target history flood in the last 1, 7, 30 days (counts) weak, but honest and cheap calendar \(\sin, \cos\) of day-of-year; monsoon_season seasonality without a discontinuity at New Year place basin one-hot; the basin's floodplain_percent, population_density_km2, vulnerability_score static context; 10 basins, so kept small

Normalisation: log1p on rainfall and the rainfall windows (heavy right tail), then standardisation of every numeric feature with train-split mean and sd. The station anomalies are already standardised by construction. One-hot columns are left as 0/1.

Feature count target: about 40. Every feature has a one-line justification in the report, and the ablation in Phase 3 removes each group in turn to show what it buys.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Classification (projects/classification/)
docs.text:
The model is the from-scratch MLP from the MLP exercise (docs/exercises/mlp/code/mlp.py), reused unchanged: layer sizes as an argument, sigmoid output, binary cross-entropy, mini-batch gradient descent. Additions the imbalance needs, implemented by hand in the same style: class-weighted cross-entropy (or oversampling of the positive class in each mini-batch) and early stopping on validation PR-AUC.

Baselines, in this order, each reported on validation and test:

  1. Majority class ("never floods") — the accuracy trap, shown once.
  2. Monsoon gate ("floods whenever monsoon_season = 1") — recall 100 %, precision 5 %.
  3. Persistence ("floods tomorrow if it flooded today").
  4. Logistic regression on the same features — the linear reference.
  5. The dataset's own flood_risk_score at \(t\) — the leaky reference, labelled as such.
  6. The MLP.

Metrics: ROC-AUC, PR-AUC (the headline), precision and recall at the chosen threshold, the confusion matrix, and a calibration curve. The threshold is set on validation for 80 % recall, and the report states the precision that buys. Training and validation loss curves per epoch.

Explainability, so every prediction can be argued with:

  • ablation by feature group (drop one group, retrain, report the PR-AUC change);
  • permutation importance on validation;
  • partial-dependence curves for the top five features (rainfall 7-day sum, river-level anomaly, soil moisture, ...), which is where the report says what the model learned;
  • error analysis: which stations, which months, and what the missed floods looked like the day before;
  • one worked example: a single station-day, its feature vector, and the probability, traced.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Generative (projects/generative/)
docs.text: Scoped after Phase 3. The candidate: a variational autoencoder over 14-day windows of the four measurements, to synthesise plausible pre-flood sequences and to score anomalies, evaluated against the monsoon-season distribution of real windows.

docs.title: Definition of done, per phase
docs.text: A phase is done when its page has every required section from the course statement, every number in the text matches its script's output, every figure has a title, axis labels and a legend, the scripts run from a clean checkout with the dataset in place, and the site builds.

docs.title: 1. EDA — Will this station flood tomorrow?
docs.text:
Project: ASIA-FLOOD 25-Year Flood Risk Atlas · Task: binary classification · Target: flood_event_occurred on day t+1, for the same station

Team: Luigi Lopes · Lucas Abatepietro · Marcelo Alonso

This is the first deliverable of the classification project: an exploratory analysis of the dataset that will be used until the end of the semester, ending in a preprocessing pipeline ready for modelling. No model is trained here.

The question is asked at 456,550 station-days: given everything a river monitoring station has recorded up to and including day t, will it report a flood on day t+1?

docs.title: 0. Proposal
docs.text:
Dataset ASIA-FLOOD: 25-Year Flood Risk Atlas (2000–2024) Source Kaggle, by aliahmadmphil Licence CC BY-SA 4.0 Size 456,600 rows × 21 columns (station_daily_data_full.csv) Task Classification — will station s flood on day t+1? Target flood_event_occurred, shifted one day forward within each station Features raw: 14 numerical / 6 categorical + date · modelled: 6 numerical + 2 categorical → 21 after the pipeline First risk two columns (flood_risk_score, severity_level) are the target in disguise — stage 1B quantifies it

The file carries 25 years of daily records for 50 river-monitoring stations across 10 Asian basins and 7 countries: rainfall, river level, soil moisture and temperature, plus static basin context and three outcome columns. A one-day-ahead flood warning is the natural task: it is the horizon at which a warning is still actionable, and the dataset is a daily panel built for it.

Figures are numbered by the item they belong to — Figure 3B.2 is the second figure of item 3B — so each item's figure budget is visible in the numbering itself (stage 1 and the synthesis, which have no per-item cap, are numbered sequentially: Figures 1.1–1.5 and 5.1–5.2). Every figure carries a title, labelled axes with units and a legend, and is followed by one explicit conclusion.

docs.title: 1. Initial inspection
docs.text: Stage 1 fixes the vocabulary: what is in the file, what is wrong with it, what is predicted, and which rows may be used to fit anything. Every number is printed by t1_inspection.py, which re-derives it from data/station_daily_data_full.csv.

docs.title: A. Data dictionary
docs.text:
Source. ASIA-FLOOD: 25-Year Dataset (Kaggle, author aliahmadmphil), licence CC BY-SA 4.0. documentation/metadata.json declares version 3.0, 2000–2024, 456,600 records, 50 stations, 10 basins. The README says "Generated on: 2026-07-23", so the data is synthetic (see the warning at the top).

What a row is. One monitoring station on one calendar day: a balanced daily panel of 456,600 rows × 21 columns = 50 stations × 9,132 days, 2000-01-01 → 2024-12-31, with no gaps.

Six columns (year, month, day, day_of_year, season, monsoon_season) are deterministic re-encodings of date (0 mismatches on all 456,600 rows). Three (flood_risk_score, severity_level, flood_event_occurred) are outcome-derived (Section B).

Companion files. station_daily_data_full.csv (456,600 × 21) is the only data source used. station_daily_data.csv (100,000 × 21) is a uniform 21.90 % random sample of it and is not used: it keeps 21.90 % of the rows and breaks the daily time axis that lag and window features need. vulnerability_data.csv (10 × 18, one row per basin) and asia_flood_geospatial.geojson (10 basin Polygons) are static context only.

docs.title: B. Quality
docs.text:
Missing values — there are none. All 21 columns report count 0 (0.00 %): 0 of 9,588,600 cells. That is the finding: nothing to impute, and none may be claimed. An imputer in the pipeline is only a robustness guard for a future partial day.

Duplicates and panel completeness. 0 fully duplicated rows, 0 duplicated (station_id, date) pairs, 0 missing days. Every station has exactly 9,132 rows, and 50 × 9,132 = 456,600: the panel is rectangular and complete.

Figure 1.1. Panel completeness. (a) Rows per station against the expected 9,132. (b) Date coverage per station, with the three split windows marked. Conclusion: the panel is balanced and gap-free, so no station or period needs special handling.

Inconsistencies, quantified.

  1. One genuine contradiction — 32 rows. Exactly 32 rows have flood_risk_score == 7.00: all are severity_level == "Extreme" and all have flood_event_occurred == 0, because the label is the strict rule risk > 7.0 while the Extreme bin includes 7.00.
  2. soil_moisture_percent is censored at exactly 100.00 — 9,153 rows (2.0046 %), a clipping artefact, not a measurement.
  3. latitude/longitude are constants: 1 unique value per station, only 50 distinct coordinate pairs ((station_name, latitude, longitude) is duplicated on 456,550 rows). They are static metadata repeated on every row.
  4. country is redundant: basin → country is a function (10 basins, 7 countries), so it adds nothing to basin.
  5. Names contradict coordinates: the five Mekong stations are all tagged country == "Vietnam", yet "Luang Prabang" sits at 16.1453 °N 103.0213 °E, which is Thailand, not Laos. Names are decorative; the coordinates are what the file encodes.

Columns to drop, each with its reason (the single source of truth is DROPPED in code/data.py):

dropped column reason severity_level target leakage — a deterministic binning of flood_risk_score flood_risk_score target leakage / redundant — risk > 7.0 reproduces the same-day label on 456,600/456,600 rows (ROC-AUC 1.0000); r = 0.934 with soil_moisture_percent, and a weaker next-day predictor (AUC 0.8088) data_quality_score noise — |r| ≤ 0.004 against every other column (max 0.0022); next-day ROC-AUC 0.5072 station_name redundant — 1:1 with station_id country redundant — a function of basin day noise — day-of-month, r = 0.0007 with the next-day target latitude, longitude constant within station

This leaves 6 numeric inputs (rainfall_mm, river_level_m, soil_moisture_percent, temperature_celsius, day_of_year, monsoon_season) and 2 categorical ones (basin, season): 8 model features from 21 raw columns.

Leakage investigation. This is the decisive finding of stage 1.

Two columns give the answer away

On all 456,600 rows, the same-day label is exactly the threshold rule

flood_event_occurred  ==  (flood_risk_score > 7.0)

with max(risk | flood = 0) = 7.00 and min(risk | flood = 1) = 7.01: the classes are linearly separable on that one column (ROC-AUC 1.0000). severity_level is a second copy of the same information.

severity_level flood_risk_score min max rows floods Low 1.00 2.99 234,226 0 Moderate 3.00 4.99 129,974 0 High 5.00 6.99 82,479 0 Extreme 7.00 10.00 9,921 9,889 all 1.00 10.00 456,600 9,889

severity_level is cut(risk, [1, 3, 5, 7, 10.01], right=False), reproduced on 456,600 / 456,600 rows (pandas' default right=True reproduces only 450,602). The Extreme bin holds 9,921 rows but only 9,889 floods: that is the 32-row contradiction above.

Figure 1.4. The leakage audit. (a) Rows per severity_level bin, same-day floods in red: Low, Moderate and High (446,679 rows together) contain 0 floods. (b) Range of flood_risk_score per same-day class: the largest non-flood value is 7.00, the smallest flood value 7.01. (c) ROC-AUC of single raw columns: 1.0000 for the risk score against the same-day label, only 0.8088 against the next-day label — below soil moisture's 0.8364. Conclusion: the risk score is the same-day label up to one threshold (a leak); for the next-day target it is a weaker copy of columns that are already features, so excluding it loses nothing.

The nuance for a one-day-ahead target. For the same-day label these columns are leakage. For the project's target y(t) = flood_event_occurred(t+1), a value observed at t is merely stale. They are excluded anyway because they are redundant, not informative: flood_risk_score correlates r = 0.9337 with soil_moisture_percent (0.6643 with river_level_m, 0.5949 with rainfall_mm), and as a next-day predictor it scores ROC-AUC 0.8088, below soil_moisture_percent (0.8364) and barely above rainfall_mm (0.8091).

docs.title: C. Target
docs.text:
The deliverable's label is the one-day-ahead flood event,

y(t) = flood_event_occurred(t + 1)        groupby("station_id")["flood_event_occurred"].shift(-1)

Shifting drops the last day of every station (50 rows), leaving 456,550 usable rows.

count share y = 0 (no flood tomorrow) 446,661 97.834 % y = 1 (flood tomorrow) 9,889 2.166 % imbalance (negatives : positives) — 45.2 : 1

The majority-class accuracy is 97.83 %: that is the trivial baseline, stated once, and accuracy is never used again. The headline metric is PR-AUC, with ROC-AUC alongside.

Figure 1.2. Class balance of the next-day label over 456,550 usable station-days: (a) raw counts, (b) log axis (45.17 : 1), (c) class shares. Conclusion: the problem is severely imbalanced — "never floods" is 97.83 % accurate, so every metric must be read against the 2.166 % base rate.

The seasonal gate is part of the target. 0 floods occur in January–April and in November–December; 95.04 % of floods (same-day) fall in July–September (94.31 % under the next-day label, where June absorbs 92 positives). The flood rate is 5.1702 % when monsoon_season = 1 against 0.000377 % (1 flood in 265,350 rows) when it is 0 — about 13,700×. "Never flood outside the monsoon" is a free baseline, so any model must be judged inside the monsoon window, where the base rate is ~5.2 %, not 2.2 % (month-by-month in 3B).

docs.title: D. Train and test
docs.text:
A temporal split is appropriate; a stratified-random one is not.

  1. Rows one day apart are near-duplicates. Pooled within-station lag-1 autocorrelation is 0.968 for temperature, 0.820 for soil moisture, 0.772 for the risk score, 0.220 for river level, 0.162 for rainfall.
  2. A random split leaks across the boundary. With train_test_split(test_size=0.20, random_state=42, stratify=…), 1,250 of 1,250 (station, year) blocks and 9,132 of 9,132 dates appear on both sides, and 145,898 adjacent-day pairs straddle the boundary. The date-based split shares 0 dates and has 100 straddling pairs (2 year boundaries × 50 stations).

Figure 1.5. The split audit. (a) Share of (station, year) blocks and dates with rows on both sides: 100.0 % (random) against 0.0 % (chronological). (b) Adjacent-day pairs across the boundary: 145,898 against 100 (1,459× fewer). (c) Lag-1 autocorrelation of the features. Conclusion: a random split would put near-copies of training rows in the test set, so its score would measure memorised neighbours rather than forecasting skill.

The split adopted (SPLITS in code/data.py) is chronological, by date, identical dates for every station, with the seed fixed at random_state = SEED = 42 for every stochastic step (sampling, PCA, t-SNE, UMAP).

split years rows usable (next-day) floods next-day rate stations train 2000–2016 310,500 6,566 2.1147 % 50 validation 2017–2020 73,050 1,620 2.2177 % 50 test 2021–2024 73,000 1,703 2.3329 % 50

The test year window holds 73,050 rows, but the 50 last-day rows (2024-12-31) have no t+1, leaving 73,000 usable; 310,500 + 73,050 + 73,000 = 456,550.

Figure 1.3. Flood days per year 2000–2024 (bars) and annual flood rate (line), with the three windows shaded. Conclusion: flood counts are stable across all 25 years (minimum 354, maximum 439, mean 395.6), so a chronological split has no regime change to trip on. There is a mild upward drift (2.0820 % in 2000, 2.3716 % in 2024), which is why the test rate is the one quoted as the test base rate.

Fitting discipline from here on

Every preprocessing statistic — scalers, imputers, category vocabularies, any decision threshold — is fitted on the training split only. Validation and test rows are only transformed.
